summary: Ten comment-endorsed discoveries spanning developer tools, open AI, robotics, and viewing.
telegram_footer: 10 items surfaced | 30/30 stories processed · 4,685 comments | history + run artifact updated

items.name: jsontext
items.source_story_title: A new Go API for JSON
items.summary: Go's JSON token parser; praised for fast parsing with precise error reporting.
items.why_included: A production user explicitly recommends it for non-straightforward parsing.
items.evidence: A company user praises its speed and recommends jsontext for challenging parsing requirements.

evidence_sources.author: txomon
evidence_sources.excerpt: There is no introspection and speed is superb. I would definitely recommend jsontext as a parser for anything non-straightforward.

items.name: Yori
items.summary: Windows command shell with classic styling and Unix-inspired conveniences, including autocomplete.
items.why_included: A first-hand user calls its deliberately modest Windows experience a joy to use.
items.evidence: A user enjoys Yori's polished Windows 2000 feel and autocomplete while noting it is less featureful than Kitty.

evidence_sources.author: marttt
evidence_sources.excerpt: I've been using Yori [1]. Not comparable at all to Kitty in terms of features, but a joy to use if you like a polished "Win2k feel" with only a handful of added unix-isms like decent autocomplete etc.

items.name: Crystal
items.source_story_title: A new Go API for JSON
items.summary: Compiled programming language; a new user praises the pleasure of building with it.
items.why_included: Enthusiastic hands-on approval emerged in a JSON discussion rather than a language launch.
items.evidence: A user says building in Crystal is great fun, while explicitly withholding a production-readiness judgment.

evidence_sources.author: alexfortin
evidence_sources.excerpt: It's really great fun to build stuff in Crystal, I don't have anything prod-grade yet to say how it scores there but the community seems to be happy about that too.

items.name: Gitea
items.source_story_title: Incident with Pull Requests, Git Operations and Issues
items.summary: Self-hosted Git forge; a longtime user praises easy setup, deployment webhooks, and API tooling.
items.why_included: Concrete multi-year approval supports resurfacing after the 90-day cooldown.
items.evidence: One commenter calls Gitea amazing; a replying longtime user endorses easy setup, testing and deployment webhooks, and its API browser.

evidence_sources.author: raddan
evidence_sources.excerpt: Seconded. Also very easy to set up. I’ve been running it for years, along with webhooks to kick off testing and website deployment jobs. I especially like the swagger browser that generate API calls for you to try in curl.

items.name: Jenkins
items.source_story_title: Incident with Pull Requests, Git Operations and Issues
items.summary: Self-hosted CI server; a CUDA-container builder values reliable local builds and lower costs.
items.why_included: A substantial real build workload offers a specific reason to choose local CI.
items.evidence: A user reports reliable local builds, roughly 2,000 builds last year, and no breakage despite update churn; hosted builds were too costly for their large CUDA containers.

evidence_sources.author: karolist
evidence_sources.excerpt: Same for me, ssh access was intermittent, but at least I have reliable local builds when GitHub actions is out but access works. With AI running Jenkins is not that hard. I build large cuda containers so cost alone ruled out hosted builds for my usecase. There's a bit of update churn but nothing broke so far. I ran around 2000 builds last year.

items.name: Marin
items.source_story_title: There is no posttraining data commons
items.summary: Open AI research project sharing training code, data sources, weights, and experiments.
items.why_included: A commenter explicitly praises a concrete effort toward open AI infrastructure.
items.evidence: A commenter calls Marin promising and cool in a discussion of shared posttraining infrastructure.

evidence_sources.author: mindwok
evidence_sources.excerpt: The Marin project from Stanford (and I believe now ran by Openathena, the authors of this blog post) is really promising and cool:

items.name: Stringman
items.source_story_title: Stringman, an $800 open-source room scale gripper robot
items.summary: Open-source room-scale gripper robot suspended from ceiling cables; an inventive robotics rabbit hole.
items.why_included: Independent comment enthusiasm supports inclusion beyond the submitted product announcement.
items.evidence: A commenter remains excited about Stringman after an earlier sighting, but says rental-wall constraints make buying it unlikely.

evidence_sources.author: jauntywundrkind
evidence_sources.excerpt: I saw Stringman here a couple of weeks ago & it's been hard to not thing about it! I don't own though, so, seems unlikely I'd commit, as alas the walls are not a simple white I can easily patch & paint. But so cool!

items.name: The Internals of PostgreSQL
items.summary: Free PostgreSQL internals guide; a commenter recommends starting with heap-only tuple updates.
items.why_included: A specific reading recommendation supplies a useful entry point into a substantial technical guide.
items.evidence: A commenter recommends the HOT update section, followed by zHeap and TOAST notes, to develop a mental model of PostgreSQL.

evidence_sources.author: gopalv
evidence_sources.excerpt: If you are just skimming this doc, The HoT update path is the section I would jump to. Understand HoT and then read the zHeap implementation notes (also of TOAST) puts a good mental model of what postgres does and what it doesn't do.

items.name: HackerTV
items.source_story_title: Show HN: HackerTV – HN's most-recommended Youtube videos as 24/7 TV channels
items.summary: HN-recommended YouTube videos arranged as live TV channels for serendipitous viewing.
items.why_included: A hands-on viewer explicitly prefers channel surfing to choosing individual videos.
items.evidence: A viewer calls HackerTV cooler than expected and says channel surfing is more enjoyable than picking videos.

evidence_sources.author: 5555watch
evidence_sources.excerpt: Oh damn this is much cooler than I expected! For some reason skimming through channels is more enjoyable than click a video I'd probably wouldn't click on

items.name: Tim's Vermeer
items.summary: Documentary following inventor Tim Jenison's attempt to recreate Vermeer's painting techniques.
items.why_included: An unambiguous film recommendation surfaced unexpectedly in a Halloween-costume thread.
items.evidence: A commenter heartily recommends Tim's Vermeer and links its trailer.
